## Abstract

The purpose of this review is to present a comprehensive overview of the theory of ensemble Kalman–Bucy filtering for continuous-time, linear-Gaussian signal and observation models. If A is allowed to be unstable, then the asymptotic (time-varying) stability of \((A-{{P}}_{t}\,S)\) in the classical Kalman filter follows under so-called detectability (or observability) conditions [89, 115, 139]. Detectability intricately relates the relevant rank deficient directions in \(P_t\) and S in terms of the unstable directions in A (i.e. it basically ensures those directions of A that are unstable are observed (as captured by S) and nonzero weighted in the update Kalman gain via \(P_t\)). The rank of the sample covariance \(\widehat{{P}}_{t}\) is at most \(\textsf{N}\ge 1\). If \(\textsf{N}<d\), then \(\widehat{{P}}_{t}\) is almost surely rank deficient and thus, has zero eigenvalues in some directions. In general, we cannot control the directions in which the random, sub-rank, \(\widehat{{P}}_{t}\) has zero eigenvalues (e.g. to play nicely with S in the sense of detectability). If A is unstable in those directions, the filter is consequently unstable in those directions. Thus, there is a basic, unavoidable, but also transparent tradeoff in requiring either stability of \(\textrm{Absc}(A)<0\) or sufficiently large ensemble sizes \(\textsf{N}\ge d\) in the derivation of uniform-in-time stability results for the EnKF.

In the stability results stated in this work, we emphasised unstable models A but required sufficiently large ensemble sizes \(\textsf{N}\ge d\). Nevertheless, most stability results stated in this work with the hypothesis that “\(\textsf{N}\) is sufficiently large” may be restated with this condition replaced with “\(\textsf{N}\ge 1\) and \(\textrm{Absc}(A)<0\)”, and such results hold time-uniformly over infinite time horizons. In [19, 21, 22], the details on “\(\textsf{N}\) is sufficiently large” are given more explicitly. Note some results that do not consider or rely on the long time stability behaviour of the samples, e.g. the fluctuation size of the sample covariance about its true value, hold with \(\textsf{N}\ge 1\) and any matrix A, e.g. this is true for the DEnKF in Theorem 5.4.

We remark that the assumption that the true Kalman–Bucy filter is stable in the sense \(\mu (A-{{P}}_{\infty }\,S)<0\) is used in a number of the fluctuation (on the sample mean) and long-time behavioural results given in the cited, prior, work [17, 19, 21, 22, 53]. It was originally believed by the authors that this condition was a stronger assumption than the more natural condition \(\textrm{Absc}(A-{{P}}_{\infty }\,S)<0\). The latter follows from the very natural model assumptions of detectability and stabilisability, see (2.11) and the discussion following that equation, e.g. [91, Theorems 9.12, 9.15]. However, the particular logarithmic norm \(\mu (\cdot )\) used throughout the prior work in [17, 19, 21, 22, 53] is unimportant, i.e. the matrix norm defining the log-norm can be chosen arbitrarily. From [131, Theorem 5], it is now known that if \(\textrm{Absc}(A-{{P}}_{\infty }\,S)<0\), then there exists a particular log-norm \(\mu (\cdot )\) such that \(\mu (A-{{P}}_{\infty }\,S)<0\). Thus, the conditions antecedent in much of the prior work, in which we ask for \(\mu (A-{{P}}_{\infty }\,S)<0\) can be replaced with just asking for classical detectability and stabilisability conditions. (In prior work, it was discussed and claimed by the authors that asking for \(\mu (A-{{P}}_{\infty }\,S)<0\) may be viewed as asking for a type of strong observability and controllability. This may be true if one specifies first the log-norm of interest. But if one does not care which log-norm is used, we can significantly relax the setting and simply ask for detectability/stabilisability which leads to \(\textrm{Absc}(A-{{P}}_{\infty }\,S)<0\)). Much of the analysis, as already discussed, requires \(S\in \mathbb {S}_d^+\) which automatically implies detectability (in fact a much stronger condition than observability).

We reconstruct linearized gravitational perturbations in $AdS_{4}$ from a conserved, traceless stress tensor on a fixed conformally flat boundary metric, extending our earlier real Lorentzian construction. For admissible data with no spacelike Fourier support in a flat conformal frame, the physical response reduces to an integral over boundary light-cone cuts. Boundary improvements restore Fefferman--Graham (FG) gauge while preserving normalizability and the linearized Weyl tensor. We then reconstruct perturbations with general spacelike boundary momentum, including nonzero frequency and its zero-frequency limit, using explicit position-space generalized functions on real stress data. Raw 1024 O2 and BeH2 mean residuals exceed returned uncertainty by factors 12-32. Pittsburgh BeH2 cross-job standard deviation is 5.6 times mean returned uncertainty. The zero-noise extrapolation (ZNE) package reduces O2 absolute residuals by 49.7% on Aachen and 83.5% on Pittsburgh at about fourfold charge. On Pittsburgh, twirled readout error extinction (TREX) removes 80 millihartree (mHa) per Raw 1024 job charge versus 50 mHa for ZNE. Controls reveal qubit-124 preparation or readout errors 5.4-5.6 times calibration; 13 mitigated energy point estimates fall outside the mapped spectrum, with no Raw counterpart. These results support workload checks and repeated measurements before additional sampling.

I use LLMs to forecast treatment effects of research studies pre-registered on the AEA RCT Registry and the Open Science Framework. I focus on studies whose results were first publicly released in 2026 and elicit forecasts from models whose training or knowledge cut-off dates were before the relevant set of papers was released. First, LLM models extract forecasting questions from the pre-registrations or pre-analysis plans. These questions elicit forecasted treatment effects; not all resolve in the subsequent papers, but those that do can be used to consider forecast accuracy. Forecasts were elicited for 889 treatment effects from 39 papers with results disclosed in January 2026 or later, or 673 from 33 papers after screening. Forecasts were elicited in raw units but I focus on those that could be standardized and therefore compared across papers. Currently, the median absolute forecast error is 0.054 SD for the best model, the average absolute error is 0.093 SD, and the MSE is 0.0218. The AI forecasts perform substantially better than benchmarks forecasting 0 effect or forecasting the mean effect of other papers' results in that time period. Overall, these results suggest considerable scope for forecasts to be of value in informing policy and research.

We investigate the interaction between a vanishing obstacle and the vanishing viscosity limit in the setting of the inhomogeneous incompressible Navier-Stokes equations with no-slip boundary conditions. We work in the space exterior to a small obstacle in three dimensions. We prove quantitative convergence rates, assuming that the obstacle is sufficiently small, namely smaller than a constant times the viscosity. The convergence holds as long as the solution to the limit problem is known to exist and stays sufficiently smooth. This extends the results of Iftimie, Lopes Filho and Nussenzveig Lopes to the inhomogeneous Navier-Stokes equations. Moreover, we can show improved convergence rates and convergence of the gradient in $\mathbb{R}^3$.

@misc{2610.38870, author = {Ken Ono}, title = {{A}n asymptotic {J}ensen-{P}olya criterion for {GRH}}, year = {2026}, eprint = {2610.38870}, note = {arXiv:2610.38870v1} }[Button: Copy Citation]

The Jensen--Pólya criterion expresses the generalized Riemann hypothesis (GRH) for Dedekind zeta-functions as a real-rootedness condition on their Jensen polynomials. Previous asymptotic results require large shifts, while computations establish real-rootedness in the Riemann case through a finite range of degrees. Here we study the unshifted family as the degree tends to infinity. For every number field $K$, we prove unconditionally that $J_{K,d}(X)$ is nonzero and has at least $d-C_K\sqrt{d\log d}$ distinct negative real zeros for all sufficiently large $d$, where $C_K>0$ depends only on $K$. Therefore, the proportion of real zeros tends to one with error $O_K(\sqrt{\log d/d})$. The main theorems have been autoformalized in Lean~4 by AxiomProver.
